utterances.text: Can we bring in the witness now? Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the witness enters the courtroom, I would like to use this time to introduce a new member of our team. That's Mr. Ozren Ogrizovic, our new case manager. Bojan Stefanovic, our former case manager, has left our team and gone to the US to study.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and welcome, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll make an effort to finish with you today. If not, you'll need to return again tomorrow. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We discussed yesterday some of the sources used by the Prosecution expert in making his report. I would like to ask you now: What are the relevant sources that you used in your report that were not used by Dr. Brunborg and his team?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to all the sources used by Dr. Brunborg and his associates, I also used the sources available at the Demographic Unit of the OTP related to databases of the BH Army, databases about deceased persons, DEM 2T, databases called Muslims Against Genocide, a database I was able to peruse but not to check called The Bosnian Book of Dead, as well as a series of documents disclosed by the Office of the Prosecutor. Those are only the sources that were available at the Demographic Unit of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Kindly tell us, what is the database of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH Army database is a database containing personal information about soldiers, made available by the Ministry of the Defence of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2001. That database contains a number of elements based on which one can establish the first name, last name, father's name, date of birth, identification number, affiliation, status, military or not, perhaps the military post number. I'm not expert about this area. Database Tuzla, for instance, database Sarajevo, database Mostar, for example. There are about 28.000 data about soldiers and other personnel of the BH Army. All this information is accompanied by the personal identification number of a given person.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Nikolic speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could we call this database records?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Records of military conscripts?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these are not records of military conscripts, not the way I understand the concept of military conscript. In war, it could mean anything. This is called "database of the BH Army," and I interpret it to be a database of soldiers and other personnel for a given time period. I'm not a military expert, but I would not call it "records" in the way you characterized records.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What were you able to determine on the basis of this extensive database?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By comparing this database with a list of missing and dead persons made by Dr. Brunborg and his associates, I established that there are a great number of overlaps between that database and the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the OTP list, the missing in Srebrenica, that contains 7.661 persons from 2005?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "Dr. Brunborg's list," I always mean the OTP's list called "The Missing and Dead" related to Srebrenica, containing 7.661 [Realtime transcript read in error "6.061"] persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In order to establish the existence of a soldier in this OTP list, which method did you use?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I applied the same method as the experts of the Prosecution, the method of matching, with a proviso that I did not use as many criteria for matching. I used only two possible keys for matching. I checked how many soldiers could be matched from the Prosecution list if I had used a greater number of keys. I want to emphasise one thing. When I use the word "key" for matching, that means a number of elements that make up one key. I used the key that says "name, surname, father's name, date of birth." That's one criterion. So these four elements make up one key, that is, one criterion. If I do the matching using that criterion, I get a little over 2.000 soldiers. If I loosen that criterion a bit, using name, surname, father's name, and just the year of birth, so again there are four elements, but the reliability of matches is a bit looser because there may be people who were born in the same year and have the same name and surname, if I use that key, I get 3.277, or perhaps 3.377.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We'll look at that document. Just one correction in the transcript. Page 6, line 11, it said "6.061 persons." It should be "7.661 persons." May we now call up in e-court 3D398A, attachment A -- attachment 1, page 1, and 3D398B, page 1. If we could have them in parallel on the screen. Those are various findings of the expert, and Dr. Radovanovic could explain how she obtained them. 3D398A, that's attachment 1, page 1, and 398, attachment 2, page 1. Professor, we are getting on our screens the two attachments. Would you be able to read the headings? Page 1, please, for both attachments.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try, although it's very small.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have hard copies with me that can be handed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I really can't see anything here. If you could perhaps zoom in. We don't need to see the whole table. I just need to see the heading. Thank you. On the left, if I can see right, we see data on matched soldiers from the Prosecution list, using the key, including name, surname, father's name and date of birth. And you can see that these are the same names, same surnames, same father's name, same date of birth. I emphasise "date of birth." And here we have columns headed: "Date of Disappearance," or "Date of Death," from the Prosecution list, as opposed to the date of death given by the army. The last column is the personal identification number of citizens. The personal identification number of citizens is a number consisting of 13 digits, and according to the laws of the former Yugoslavia, it was introduced in 1982. The personal identification number, the seven digits -- the first seven digits represents the date, month, and year of birth. The next digit is the area of former republic; for instance, Serbia was 7, Bosnia-Herzegovina was 8, Croatia was 1. The following three digits represent the sex of the person given that identification number. Anything over 500 means female. Everything below 500 is male. And there is another digit which defines not only the republic but the locality issuing the personal ID. I cannot tell you now exactly about localities, but if the ID was given out in Sarajevo, it will be 1. If it was issued in Banja Luka, this digit will be 2. Since personal IDs are issued by the Secretariat of Personal Affairs, it is possible to establish exactly which locality issued the card. And then there is a digit which is a verification number. There is a certain number for verifying the personal identification number, because, in principle, there should not exist two identical personal identification numbers. Every number should be unique, and there should not be two persons with the same personal ID number. This unique number is an identification used by many services in many documents, so you don't need the name and surname. It is amply sufficient to establish the identity of the person. The other table is the same kind of match, but with a looser criterion that does not take into account the date of birth, but just the year of birth. According to that second criterion, it is possible to match almost 1.000 persons more. In my report, I say that using a broad criterion, it's possible to match around 5.000 persons, but saying that, I'm trying, in fact, to emphasise the importance of the key used for matching, because if, within one research project, within one study, you change the elements in the identification key, then you open the door wide to speculation and you decrease the reliability of the finding.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We won't be needing this document any longer, unless you have something to add about these two attachments, Professor.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only draw your attention to this: The data contained in these columns are taken over from originals. You will notice that in one column the listing goes "Day, Month, Year," in another listing it's "Month, Day, Year." That should not confuse you. Those are exactly the same pieces of information. I just transposed them here from the original, as they were originally listed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your report, on page 5, in paragraph 5, you listed all the sources that you have told us earlier today the Prosecution had not used in making their report, and there you said that there is no explanation why all these sources were not taken into account, although they are equal or better in quality compared to those used, and that has significantly affected the objectivity of the objectivity of the findings. The first source are the records of BH Army servicemen killed during 1992-1995 conflict. We have evidence here on transcript page 6.807, lines 19 through 25, evidence given by Demographer Brunborg, saying that Prosecution experts, in order to establish who got killed before 1995, consulted lists of soldiers killed. I want to ask you: In your research, when you were making the report, and later, did you come across information that Dr. Brunborg used the lists of the BH Army in making his report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's not a single report where Mr. Brunborg or his associates, but in the Srebrenica report there is no mention of the use of the BH Army sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of July, 2008, the Defence received from the Prosecution some materials. That was last Friday. That's demographic material, a letter from Madam Ewa Tabeau, entitled "The Matching of the Military Records of the BH Army," with the Prosecution's list of the missing from Srebrenica in 2005. That's document 3D457 in e-court. In preparing for this testimony, did you inspect this document and its annexes?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Is this the first time that you see that the Prosecution demographers used the BH Army database in their analyses concerning Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first time concerning Srebrenica, but one of the whole authors of the Srebrenica report, the one from 2005, Dr. Ewa Tabeau, did use the BH Army database in the report on Sarajevo, that was in the Galic case, I testified in that trial, too, in order to identify soldiers versus civilians, because that was at issue at the time in the Galic case. That was the demographic report in the Galic case. So in 2002, the report that was drafted by Dr. Ewa Tabeau does list among the sources the BH Army database and also the Muslims Against Genocide, among other sources.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could the counsel please switch off the microphones while the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Madam Nikolic, did you hear what the interpreters suggested; namely, that while the witness is speaking, you should keep your microphone switched off.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I do apologise to the interpreters if I have caused them any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to the previous page of this document, where we have an explanation for the direct and indirect method. This is what the professor has just told us about and where we have the exact figures. So that would be the previous page in the English version, and perhaps I think it's page 2 -- the next page in B/C/S. So that would be page 1 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S. Here we have the text in bold, where it says: "Indirect approach," and: "Direct approach."

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Professor, is this what you've just been telling us about?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I've been telling you about, but let me underline here, I think it's a way of translation or a different way of thinking, but if we're talking about matching, there is no direct and indirect approaches. You have a database, and have you to define your key. So generally speaking, the first approach is where you have the matching key, which is the personal ID numbers, you have two sources, the list of soldiers from the BH Army, and the census list, and then you have the matches. The second key is the element -- the attributes such as first name, last name, father's name, date of birth, and you have again the BH Army list and the Prosecution list, and here you have the different number of matches, which is 4.964. I apologise. Let me finish, please. Ms. Tabeau here presents a conclusion that I really can't read here. She says this finding proves a very high consistency of the direct and indirect approaches. I cannot agree with this conclusion, either. This example, it's a textbook example of how changing a key or the criterion that you use to match your data yields different results. This does not confirm that if you do something using one key, there is also the other key. So to my mind, this conclusion is phrased in a way that is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The annex 1, the table in this document, it's again the same number, 3D457. If you could just zoom in a little bit. That's page 4 in e-court. We're still on the same document. "Annex 1," that's the title. It's an attachment to Ms. Tabeau's letter. That's page 4 in the English version. We don't have the B/C/S version. Thank you. Professor, in preparing for your testimony, did you see those documents that were disclosed to us by the Prosecution, including this annex?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us, as much as you can, this table?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table. Well, first of all, I would like you to give me the end of the table. Here it says that this was a comparison between the BH Army list and persons identified using DNA analysis, and Ms. Tabeau states that there are 5.198 matches here and that 4.705 of these were in Srebrenica area or, in other words, that the matches with the identified persons are as high as 73 per cent. So among the identified persons listed here, well, I don't want to now go commenting about the figures and the meaning of the word "identified," and so on, but at any rate, according to her, there are 73 per cent of the soldiers that are identified here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like us to move on to another database that you used in working out your findings. That's the DEM 2T. So could you please explain to us, what is DEM 2T as a database?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to an order of the Tribunal in The Hague, the Bureau of Statistics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Bureau of Statistics of Republika Srpska gathered data about deaths in the period between 1992 and 1995. This research was done in accordance with the rules of statistics. I think that the findings were submitted to the Tribunal in The Hague in 2004. This database contains all the persons recorded as having died between 1992 and 1995, regardless of the cause of death. In other words, if they are natural deaths or violent deaths. There are over 140.000 cases, 75.000 or 78.000 persons -- well, I can give you the precise data once I've consulted the papers -- were registered as natural deaths, and the remaining cases are violent deaths. And there are causes of deaths in -- for natural deaths in about one half of the cases. This base -- database was done by professionals, and it was submitted to the Tribunal in The Hague. I don't know -- I've never read anywhere any assessments or evaluations of the quality of this database, but I consider it significant precisely because this is an official data source, and I think that this official data source should have been used -- should have been compared with the Prosecution list, because it could improve the quality if you ascertain that if you try to match it, you encounter some cases that can be either excluded or included. That's immaterial. I quote from a table in my report where it is apparent that there is an inconsistency between the Prosecution list and this official database, because you can see that there are same persons listed there, if you apply the key, the matching key, but it is now controversial. You don't know whether these people died or should be in the Prosecution list, because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could the microphones please be switched off at Defence bench. We cannot hear the witness because of the background noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can see Ms. Nikolic's microphone is switched off. No? It was on. I see, I see, I see. Thank you. Yes, sorry for the interruption, and thank you, Madam Interpreter. Let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just briefly like to explain the principle for gathering information about death rates in statistics, what is the methodology. Data is gathered on the basis of questionnaires that contain a number of questions. Those questionnaires contain more questions than the information that is contained in the death registries. The sources for the mortality data are the death registry books. No death can be registered in the registry book if you don't have a death certificate. Death certificates are kept in perpetuity, they are kept in archives. One death certificate is kept with the register, and it is kept in perpetuity, or 100 years from now someone can go there and consult those death certificates. The other certificate is sent to the statistics bureau. There is a physician who knows how to code the death in accordance with the cause and other elements, or it can be sent to other institutions contracted by the Bureau of Statistics, where there are physicians who are able to code the deaths appropriately. Why am I saying this? Because there is this distinction between the natural and violent deaths and because the principle of how the data is collected is the same; registry books. And the DEM 2T database bears the same designation as the official statistics for the mortality, so we have the same designation, DEM 2 in statistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is yet one source that the Prosecution experts did not use, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to look at 3D398. It's in e-court. Page 21 in e-court. That's table 3 of the findings reached by Professor Radovanovic. In B/C/S, that's page 21. In English, it's page 22. I apologise, it's actually 23 in English, I have been told. Thank you, I think that's it. Professor, you have in front of you table 3. If you have any problems --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you allow me, this is a table from my report. Can I consult it in the hard copy of my report, table 3? That's what I have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't think it's going to be a problem. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. This is -- this table shows examples where there is a discrepancy between the date and place of death, between the DEM 2 database and the Prosecution list. The Prosecution list contains 7.661 persons. The last name, the first name, and the father's name are identical in both the DEM 2T database and the Prosecution list. The first column, "Date of Birth," is taken from the Prosecution list. The second column is the date of birth as recorded in the DEM 2 list. The next column is the date of death or disappearance listed by the Prosecution. And then we have the date of death recorded in the DEM 2. Then we have the place of disappearance listed by the Prosecution in its list that contains 7.661 persons, and the place of death from the DEM 2 database. You will see discrepancies that are particularly prominent when it comes to the date of death for three persons, for instance, because, for instance, the second, third and fourth persons in this list have the date of death as collected by a specialised institution. The dates are from April 1995 - that's the first person - but then you have April 1993 for the second person, and May 1995 for the third person. I'm using these persons as an example to show how, if we were to compare this with a DEM 2T base, you could, to say the least, face a dilemma whether these are really persons listed on the list as missing or dead. And the date is listed as the 12th of July, 1995, for all of them. The first person is interesting, from my point of view, because we have the same date of death, the 12th of July, 1995, but the place of death is Sarajevo, whereas on the Prosecution list the place of disappearance is listed as Buljim.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Professor, I failed to mention that this should not be made public, this table, because --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not naming any of the persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I know that you are not, but we can see it on our screens, and those names should not be made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have we been broadcasting or not? Yes, then you need to attend to it. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Professor. You said the date of death are identical. Could you check it once again, whether they are identical, in the case of the first one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12th July and the 17th of July. No, it's not identical. I'm sorry. According to the Prosecution, the date of death is the 12th of July. According to DEM 2, it's the 17th of July. The place of disappearance, according to Prosecution, is Buljim. According to DEM 2, it's Sarajevo. I'm just listing these as indicative samples to show that if the database DEM 2T had been used as well, it would have at least sown a doubt as to whether the list of people made by the Prosecution of 7.661 persons is really so reliable, as the report claims, as Srebrenica victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We can remove this document from the screen. Professor, I would like to move to a different database, another one that you used in your report, and that is the list of persons displaced from Srebrenica in 1995. Would you please tell us, what kind of database is this?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the documentation disclosed by the Office of the Prosecutor, I found two documents; one made by the World Health Organisation and another made by the UN, a sector for civil military operations. Both relate to population displaced from Srebrenica, although one document is dated 29 July 1995 and the second one is dated 4 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Professor. Let us call up these two documents in e-court. And while you are explaining, the Chamber will be able to look at them. 3D408, page 1, and 3D374, page 2 in English. If they could be put in a split screen, both of them, 3D408, English page 1, and 3D374, English page 2. They will soon be both up on our screens.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're still waiting for the second one. This one [indicates] is a document of the WHO dated 29th July 1995, and it provides -- the lettering is very small, I can't see the numbers, but I'll try -- it gives us a total number of people displaced from Srebrenica -- okay, this is much better -- and it also gives us a distribution of, you know, private accommodation, collective centres, et cetera. And the number listed is 34.341. The other document, dated 4 August 1995, also deals with displaced persons from Srebrenica, although it gives us a different total. Then WHO, again with a breakdown by accommodation, private accommodation, collective centres, et cetera. Both these documents give totals around 34.000 persons. When seeing this, I tried to find lists of these people, and in the material disclosed I came across four lists with different totals of persons. All these contain name, surname, father's name, and year of birth. My assistants integrated these lists into one single list that contained 34.537 persons, and with this aggregated list I proceeded to compare it with the Prosecution list of 7.661 persons. This attempt to match yielded several dozen persons that match, in terms of name, surname, father's name, and year of birth. That's also an indicator that shows us a certain lack authenticity. At least it's a warning that we cannot take the Prosecution list for granted. We cannot take it, based on the OTP list, that these people are really dead. Dr. Brunborg, for instance, when he doesn't find a match in the list of voters, concludes that all these persons on his lists are probably dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 3D398, annex 5. It's the finding of Professor Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You already said that you tried to match the list of missing and dead from Srebrenica with data about displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And 985. 3983E -- 3D398E, annex 5. That's the document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I see it. These are just examples. Maybe the heading is not very clear. It's examples of matches between "B," Brunborg, and "R," for displaced persons. These are just examples. I found, both in the displaced list and in the OTP list, certain persons with these names, with these surnames, with these father's names, and born in these years. So using this key, you will find absolute matches. That is again a warning that by reducing the number of elements within the identification key, you always open the door to your own subjective decisions, whether these are indeed those same persons or not. I can make a decision and say, yes, these people are matches, or, no, they are not. I have certain elements, certainly. The question is whether these elements are sufficient for me to claim, with a high degree of certainty, that those are these same identical people. This is just another example that changing the key, using a large number of criteria and few elements within a key, cannot yield scrupulously-correct results.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On this topic, I have just one more question. Based on your study, on the Prosecution list of missing and dead, did you establish whether all these persons existed in reality?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my point of view, it's a bit complex. I'll try to explain. On the Prosecution list, from my study, there are a number of non-existent persons, but let me first define "non-existent person," a conditional definition, to be able to explain this more clearly. Within the number of non-existent persons, there are some persons that Dr. Brunborg himself says, "I did not find matches in the list of population." There are 1.030 such persons -- or 13 persons [as interpreted], Brunborg says. If the method used by the Prosecution expert is geared at proving that somebody's alive and that they existed in 1991, by matching with a population list from 1991, and Dr. Brunborg failed to find matches for 13 per cent persons, then it means that these persons did not exist, according to Dr. Brunborg's methodology, and then the right thing would be to exclude them from the study. That's one category of non-existent persons. Another type of non-existent persons, let me call them fictional, are those persons that Dr. Brunborg was able to match with the list of population, but they don't necessarily have anything to do with Srebrenica or they don't have anything to do with Srebrenica. There's a number of people who died before the 10th of July, 1995. In our case, they are conditionally fictional, because they -- although they do exist in reality, but they pertain to another period. Also, there is a number of persons who, territorially speaking, although we don't have a definition even of what Srebrenica is, but these people cannot territorially be identified as Srebrenica victims. These people, too, exist in reality, but for our purposes, they are fictional. Such persons amount to 1.000, approximately, according to Dr. Brunborg himself, and another thousand are fictional, for our purposes. The professional thing to do would be to exclude them from our study. What is particularly confusing to me is this: Once Dr. Brunborg established that over 13 per cent were not identified in the list of population, so he himself decided that 13 per cent were not identified, he should have excluded them. However, instead of excluding them, Dr. Brunborg proceeds to distribute all these persons across municipalities, and then he says between 500 and 700 of these persons shall be placed in Srebrenica. Based on what facts? If you did not match them with the population list, you don't know whose residents they were? How do you know they should fall into Srebrenica? Not only does he distribute them across territory, but in later tables that he makes, where he includes age ranges, et cetera, he again places them in Srebrenica, and I'm just talking about those people that Dr. Brunborg himself found conditionally to be non-existent. Of course, this increases not only the figures themselves but also relative comparative findings, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: To sum up what you've just said, compared to the Prosecution list of 7.661 persons, what is the minimum of such non-existent persons?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we take into account what Dr. Brunborg says, 13 per cent, and if we take into account what is factually numerically proven to be fictional, then it would be one-fourth, one-fourth of 7.661.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, page 22, line 7, "13 persons," I take it that those should read "13 per cent."

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Kwon. I have just been told the same thing. Thank you for this. It should be corrected. And, again, with the table we have on the screen, it should not be seen by the public, because personal information of certain persons is included.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Professor Radovanovic, can we now discuss the methodology of work? Can you tell us about your methodology that you used in your report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wish to say that we have already discussed some aspects of methodology. The choice of sources is the first step in methodology, and so far we have been indeed discussing sources of information. The methodology that I used is identical to the methodology applied by Dr. Brunborg and his associates. It's just that I used the methodology according to all the rules of the science of statistics and practice of statistics. There is no difference in methodology; it's all about conformity with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something about special and statistical units. What does that mean, and what are the possibilities for manipulation?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I proceed with this explanation about spatial and statistical units, I want to define my bearings professionally. We are working with a very sensitive subject here, victims, and I define them professionally as statistical units. I sympathise most profoundly with every victim, and I beg your understanding when I refer to them as statistical units. It is only due to my professional approach. In statistical and demographic research, it is of crucial importance to define the space, the area you are working with. Why? Because that space delimits the population that you need to study. If you have not defined the space, the area, then you again open the door for speculation. What is Srebrenica, territorially speaking? Nowhere has it been defined in the Prosecution expert report. And when you read the reports from year 2000 through the last one, the latest one, you come across various possibilities of what Srebrenica is meant to be. Srebrenica can be just the town of Srebrenica. That's what Dr. Brunborg says. Srebrenica can be the area that comprises 13 municipalities. Srebrenica can be only the Srebrenica municipality, comprising 71 population centres. Srebrenica is also sometimes defined as an enclave, but nobody says exactly what that enclave is. So there can be no statistical or demographic study if you are not clear about the area from which you are collecting data and why these statistical units belong precisely in that area. So territorially speaking, there is not a single definition up to now. Dr. Brunborg was entitled to define Srebrenica as he saw fit, of course, but there is no such thing. So that's why if you look at all the reports, there is a certain flexibility, elasticity to the territory. When statistical units have to be gathered, and those statistical units are ambiguously defined, then Srebrenica is an area comprising 13 municipalities, including the 3 municipalities in Serbia. When these statistical units are to be distributed territorially in order to obtain very important statistical indicators, then they are distributed in an area that covers five municipalities. And since this territory is so elastic, this opens the door to manipulations. It is my belief, in light of the knowledge and experience of Dr. Brunborg, the reason why there is no definition of the territory is because Dr. Brunborg decided that Srebrenica shall be all those areas where you have persons that have gone missing between July and December 1995. So instead of a spatial definition, you have a temporal definition, so that would be the literal interpretation. What you need to do is you need to take out all the persons that have gone missing or were killed in the period between July and December 1995 from the ICRC database, and then I can decide whether I can include persons from Valjevo who are -- that's 150 kilometres away, other cases from Bijeljina or Rogatica, and so on. It's a temporal definition of an event instead of a spatial definition, where you're then supposed to put statistical units based on certain categories. This is completely adapted to the purpose of the research of Mr. Brunborg, and it has nothing to do with the scientific approach, which dictates that you have to define your territory in order to be able to see what population you're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court Exhibit P2413. That's Mr. Brunborg's report, page 34 in B/C/S, English version 29. That's table 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Professor, you have in front of you table number 11. That's from Mr. Brunborg's expert report. The date is 2005. So could you please explain to us, what is this?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table is the only analytical table in all the reports produced by Dr. Brunborg. All the other tables are tables where he presents his findings. This should be an analytical table for a very simple reason; because it provides some comparisons between various states. And this should be the crown of the report, because it talks about the proportion of deaths found by Dr. Brunborg. The first thing that is incorrect, professionally, is the fact that you don't have the absolute figure anywhere. In my opinion, that's because Dr. Brunborg fails to identify or to define his territory. Had he defined his territory, he would have said, Okay, now Srebrenica includes this population from 1991, or something that would be even more important for us, from our point of view. Dr. Brunborg says that in some documents he found that there were about 40.000 people living in Srebrenica. Not going into whether this figure was 40.000, less or more, from our aspect, from where I sit, it's immaterial. What is important is if we have the 40.000 people who are assumed to have lived in Srebrenica, what calculations were done on the basis of that? Since we don't have the population figures, Mr. Brunborg uses data from 1991, and if you compare data from a certain period of time with the information data from another time period, that's completely proper, methodologically, but Dr. Brunborg is not comparing just absolute figures. He breaks down this population by age groups, so he presents the age structure for 1995. And from the title of the table, we can see that he is doing that in relation to the persons of the same age from 1991. So he says "total population per age group" in 1995, the same thing in 1991. Since he doesn't have the information about the population in 1995, Dr. Brunborg commits a methodological error which I term "apples and oranges" principle. I may be wrong, but at any rate there is no such thing as the calculations based on apples and oranges. Of course, I was trying to be a little bit ironical here, but what does it mean if we apply it to this table, apples and oranges, and why we don't have the absolute figures listed here? If you have the population broken down by age in 1995, in order to calculate the percentages, for instance, population aged between 10 and 14, the proportion of dead or missing is 0.4, so I have the age in 1995. Now I would have to compare this with the overall population broken down in the same manner in 1991. This structural piece of information, if it is not confined in this manner, is unusable, from the point of view of methodology. What does it mean? Now I've calculated for a segment of a population, of a known population, what age they were in 1991 and 1995, and now I'm trying to ascertain the age at 1995 and what is the proportion in the population of 1991. This is simplified, of course, but statistics is a science of mass populations. For instance, Svetlana Radovanovic was between the age of 41 and 44 in 1991. I would have liked that, although it is not true. But the very same Svetlana Radovanovic, in 1995, is four years older, so she moves into a different age group, the age group between 45 and 49. Dr. Brunborg now takes this Svetlana Radovanovic from 1995, and he doesn't look for her in the parallel age group, because he doesn't have the information for 1991, but he compares Svetlana Radovanovic with an age group that she does not belong to. This is, methodologically speaking, improper, and it cannot yield results that could be considered even minimally reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Nikolic, can I draw your attention to the e-court. Does it show the correct B/C/S version or the English version is wrong?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't want to interrupt the professor. The B/C/S version is not correct, but Professor Radovanovic understands English and was able to explain this table to the Trial Chamber. But we have the correct table on the left-hand side. We don't have the correct page in B/C/S. We only have some graphs. But I didn't want to interrupt the professor. At any rate, thank you very much, Professor. So the page is 29 in English. Could we now move on to a different exhibit. This is a comparison using the example from Potocari, from your findings, that 3D398, pages 32 in B/C/S. In English it is 33 and goes on to 34. That's table 8 in Professor Radovanovic's report, 32 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Nikolic please speak into the microphone or turn on the other microphone to her right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise to the interpreters. Could we please zoom in on table 8, because we would need to see table 9 from Helge Brunborg's report in parallel. Now, I don't know how this can be done, since we now have four documents because we have both tables in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you could first talk about table 8 and then go on to discuss table 9 of Dr. Brunborg. But at any rate, have you in front of you your table 8. You analysed the principle and methodology using the example of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an example that shows that if you took absolute figures from the 1991 census and the findings about the places of disappearance, I'm using Potocari here because Professor Brunborg only presents data for the whole of Srebrenica, for Potocari and for the forest. I took the data from the official census, population census from 1991, broken down by age group. That's the official results for Potocari. This is the first column, and it says here the 1991 census. The second column is the findings of the Prosecution for the missing and the dead, and we have the total figure. Again, by age group, according to the data that Dr. Brunborg presented in table 6A, I think. So we see the absurd thing here. This is particularly present when you have small figures. If you have hundreds of thousands, millions and so on, perhaps it would not be so glaring, but if we apply Dr. Brunborg's methodology using the age groups from 1991 and comparing them with the age groups from 1995, then you would have some absurd situations. I note once again that we are talking about the dead and the missing by place, so you will see that a greater number of people went missing in a certain age group than actually existed in the same age group in 1991. And so we see those absurd results that are presented here by way of an example.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The table?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The first column shows the percentages for the total number of dead and missing, and the second one only for those who were really ascertained to have died. And since Dr. Brunborg has committed yet another error or omission, in my view, he treats all the persons missing or dead as dead, although he does have data for persons who were really certified dead. So we have here missing and dead and the data for dead alone, and there are differences in the percentages. The percentages show that there was a wrong methodological approach that was adopted here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, this could be a good time for a break. We have two minutes left, but I have maybe four or five questions to ask and then I will complete my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Nikolic, we'll have a 30-minute break starting from now. We'll reconvene at 10 past 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, I waited to see whether there would be any developments, but Judge Stole won't be able to make it today, so we'll continue sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Ms. Nikolic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Professor Radovanovic, to save time, we put both tables for Potocari during the break up on the screen. On the right, we see table 8. That's the one from your expert report. And on the left side, it's table 9B, Potocari table, from Dr. Brunborg's report.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said it already, when we didn't see the table. This table B, Potocari, Dr. Brunborg breaks down the population gone missing in Potocari by age groups from 1995, and he calculates certain percentages, and he interprets them in his own way. The information from table B has been taken over into my table 8 in their entirety, in absolute terms, but I also added data from 1991 in order to show the methodological error involved; namely, data cannot be compared in this way if they were not reduced to the same moment in time. I don't know if I managed to explain this well, but Svetlana Radovanovic, aged such-and-such in 1995, cannot be sought in a category of population that is four years younger. So I just wanted to show that this was a table where age groups were derived for Potocari and for the forest, plus totals for everything that Dr. Brunborg considers to be Srebrenica, that is, five municipalities. Professionally, it would be right if you are giving percentages and if you are considering Srebrenica to consist of five municipalities. In the key table 11, you should list absolute numbers and your own information so that we can see, on the basis of which state of the population, because we don't know what was the case in 1994. Dr. Brunborg says that one-fourth is from Srebrenica and half of the population from 39 to 44 fell victim, and on this basis he makes the conclusion of enormous casualties and great tragedy. I'm not saying that there was no tragedy. I'm just saying that the numbers arrived at by Dr. Brunborg are methodologically compromised. They were not derived in a methodologically proper way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 3D398 in e-court. That's page 30 in B/C/S and 32 in English, table 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Professor, when we see these tables, in fact, you can explain before that. What is a correct methodological approach and what this table 6 represents?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean table 6 in my report?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, in your report.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Table 6 in my report also represents an example of how, relative to the total population, it would have been intellectually and professionally correct to show these percentages. Table 6 shows how many Bosniaks there were in total in 1991 in all the five municipalities. I'm taking only these five municipalities taken by Dr. Brunborg to be Srebrenica. Then how many of this total of Bosniaks are men? And there's one error here. It says "55.000," sorry, "559.000." It's in fact 59.000. This is a typo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Professor. I don't think the figures were recorded properly in the transcript. Just a moment. Please explain this mistake in the second column.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second column, Bosniak men, it says "559.258." It's a typographical error. It's in fact 59.258. The first digit, "5," should not be there. According to the data indicated in Dr. Brunborg's report, closed cases total of 2.372, and the search was still going on for 2.389. I have already emphasised that Dr. Brunborg always shows the missing and the dead as one and the same category. It's not one and the same category. It should be professionally correct to separate these two categories. If you were to compare that to the total population, you would get that relative to the total population of what Dr. Brunborg takes to be Srebrenica, in fact, not even the total population but only Bosniaks, 4.5 per cent would be missing, whereas those cases that are considered to be closed, resolved, in the total population there would be 4 per cent of these, and if you take only men into consideration, Bosniak men, then we would say it's 9 per cent missing among the Bosniak male population. I have to say one more thing. Total Bosniaks, 1991, that's the first column, that's all Bosniaks without reference to age, all Bosniaks from zero age, and that is also professionally correct, because Mr. Brunborg makes his calculations, I think, in the age group starting with 15, or 15 to 19. He only takes into account the male population that does not take into account one-third of the population; namely, the age group from 0 to 14. This category exists, and it has to be taken into account in the numbers when such relevant figures are given. You cannot just ignore the presence of this population. I think that table 11 precisely, due to various attempts to wriggle out of the fact that one does not know the population in 1995 or 1994, and the fact that what does exist in the 1991 census is not represented correctly, in the key analytical table we have no absolute numbers. What is shown are only relative numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Table 11 of Dr. Brunborg's report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's the only table that I consider as an analytical table. It can be qualified as analytical, but I also believe it to be a kind of statistical exhibitionism, because if you don't have the elements on the basis of which you are able to establish whether your calculations are correct, then there's always a doubt that you are hiding something. We cannot check, we cannot establish, and we cannot take without reservation that one-third of Srebrenica's men fell victim, either as missing or as dead, if we don't know what it is one-third of. We have to bear in mind that the number of the population in 1991 and the population in Srebrenica, whatever "Srebrenica" means, in 1995 are completely different things, not only in quantitative terms but also in qualitative terms. In 1991, we have the number and the quality. We see the age structure, and the age structure gives us a certain quality of the population. However, in table 11 of Dr. Brunborg's, we see some sort of quality, but we don't know relative to what quantity. So it would have been professionally fair to see relative to what this calculation was made. We can only have a vague idea about that from the heading of the table, table 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I call up in e-court 3D398. It's again Professor Radovanovic's report, pages 31 in B/C/S and 32-33 in English. That's table 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this document, my question to you would be: Did you perform a correct analysis for Bratunac, Zvornik, Han Pijesak, Vlasenica municipality, applying the correct methodology, all the municipalities that Dr. Brunborg also deals with?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's another example of what would have been the professionally fair way of showing a table. This table does not suggest that my findings are scrupulously correct and accurate. I'm just trying, through this table to say that Dr. Brunborg, if he had broken down the population for 1991, and if he had broken up the categories instead of saying that the missing and the dead are one and the same category, and if he had done it methodologically properly, and if he had matched it methodologically properly, he would have obtained completely different results. I am not claiming these are the most reliable data in the world, but I am claiming that with the criterion that I'm using, these results may be obtained. Table 7 shows the findings about the missing and the dead, and their proportion in total population, according to Dr. Brunborg, and the findings that I obtained by matching names, surname, father's name and year of birth, when I compared the list of Dr. Brunborg with the list of the population. So according to that criterion containing the elements I enumerated, it is possible, in all five municipalities, to match 3.225 residents, and then we see how many relate to Srebrenica, how many to Bratunac, how many to Vlasenica, et cetera, by their place of permanent residence, since at that moment, because I spent seven days doing this and it's a huge amount of work, you are dealing with a great number of rubrics, and by that I mean listing a great number of personal information in one line for each resident, I could only see in this work what is correct. I could not see, out of these 3.225, which are still treated as missing and which have been identified as dead. I proceeded from the assumption that all those that I matched have been identified as dead. Only when you have the fact that all those matched are really identified as dead, you can talk about the rates of mortality. You cannot talk about rates of mortality if you are not sure that certain people are dead, which Dr. Brunborg really does, because he takes all 7.661 persons to be dead, and he calculates the proportions of mortality for the missing and dead, which is logical nonsense. You cannot apply rates of mortality to people whom you are not sure to be dead, at least at the moment when this was done. This is just one example how different these ratios would be and how these calculations would need to have been done to be methodologically correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an example? For example, in Srebrenica, to interpret this table?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his table, Dr. Brunborg talks about the municipality of Srebrenica and says that the mortality rate has been calculated as 33.9 per cent, which means that about 34 per cent of the total population, according to Dr. Brunborg's findings, fell victim in Srebrenica in proportion to the year 1991. He excluded -- if he had excluded everything that he was not sure about and if he started from the real mortality rate, based on the facts, on those who were established, that the result would have been completely different and it would be about 12 per cent. And that would apply to every municipality, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If we were to look at the total, the overall result?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The overall result, in comparison with what most of Dr. Brunborg considered to be Srebrenica, with respect to the five municipalities, it would result to some 6 per cent, which means that the -- a share of those male Bosniaks who were dead would amount to approximately 6 per cent in respect of the five municipalities and in respect of the total number of population in 1991. I would like to emphasise that the number of population in 1991 and the number of population which was unknown in 1995 shows a qualitative -- a difference -- a major qualitative difference. And when it comes to the quantitative characteristics, according to what Dr. Brunborg says, there were some 40.000 people, and in quantitative terms that may well be acceptable in comparison with the year 1991. But that is also something I can't be sure of, because this is just what is rumoured, and rumours are not part of the statistics and are not taken into account as part of the statistical research.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you, Professor Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. She is also your witness. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much do you think --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. About an hour, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll try not to repeat any of the questions that my learned colleague asked, and I know that you are very precise in your answers as well as in your report, and thank you for that. My first question to you, if I may, is: Do you have an opinion as to whether --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. You are speaking too fast, and the interpreters have to speed up. And for me to be able to follow you, I have to have the two things really synchronised. I apologise. Could you please slow down, and then the interpreters will slow down and I'll be able to follow you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even the witness recognised that you are incorrigible, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are unanimous and I'm grateful for assistance in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I will thank you for reminding of that. Do you have an opinion as to whether Mr. Brunborg, based on his unreasonable selection and limitations of sources utilised, his flawed methodology, and the erroneous conclusions, were result driven or result orientated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not cross. These are leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking her if she has an opinion based upon that. I think in her report it's rather clear. I think it's a fair question, and I think we -- which I could direct her to page 8 of her report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question would have been okay if you had just asked her for her opinion, but you are putting to her that Mr. Brunborg's conclusions, selections, and limitations of sources, are flawed, his methodology is flawed, his conclusions are erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was merely laying a foundation. I thought she had that in her report. I could go through it and we could come back to each of those three things, but I think does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think she has it in her report, too, but once you've got a notice from the Prosecution that they are going to object to direct questions, please -- or leading questions, then proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just have to say for the record, I don't believe that the objection is warranted, and I don't believe that it's a leading question, but I will restate the question, in the interests of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you have an opinion as to whether or not Mr. Brunborg's selection of methodology, his analysis, as well as his conclusions were in any way result driven?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that my entire report speaks about that. It is not my opinion, without any foundations. Starting with the selected source of information to the erroneous methodological procedures, when it comes to the matching of the information, when it comes to the definition of the area concerned, all these were methodological errors. So this is not my opinion. It is not that I am thinking that. This is what I established, and from my point of view they're facts to prove that the whole thing was professionally incorrect. In that, I did not try to put my opinion. I believe that Dr. Brunborg is a professional, that he has an educational background and experience to support that, and if a professional ignores such key things in professional and scientific terms, I'm not of the opinion that he will do that out of sheer ignorance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're certainly not saying that of Mr. Brunborg or any of the witnesses or scientists and demographers that the Prosecution has brought forth, but I'd like to just -- to follow up on my question, direct your attention to page 8 of your report, where I think you highlight, in the paragraph that starts with: "Age," in the middle of that paragraph, where you highlight two aspects of what you found in Mr. Brunborg's report, and you let me know when you find it, Professor, and then I'll ask you a direct question on that.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you state here with respect to Mr. Brunborg's, among other things, analysis, that it was your conclusion that it has absolutely nothing to do with scientific statistics or demography, and what I'd like to do is to elaborate on that. And just so everyone's following along, again it's page 8 of your report, which is 3D398. And you highlight two things that Mr. Brunborg states. First, and I think you have it in quotes with some text which is bold, but I'll just read it under quotes, quote: "A question is thus: How many victims must be established to convict someone of genocide?" And you thankfully have a citation to where you found that in his report. My question to you is: Is it -- have you, in your experience as a demographer, and in your educational background, and in your teaching positions, as well as the articles that you've written and published, have demographers ever been, when they do statistics or this type of work, do they first try to establish, as it says here, what is necessary in order to convict someone of a crime, much less genocide? Have you ever experienced that in your profession?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in demography there is no definition of genocide. Demography is not a science that would consider the issues of genocide and state whether one thing is genocide and the other not. Demography deals with the demographic losses that may be direct or indirect and that may have a bearing on the vital force of a certain population, but it does not determine what is or what is not genocide. So in my career, I've never had an opportunity -- I know that there is no definition of genocide, which obviously doesn't mean that none among colleagues dealt with genocide. And here Dr. Brunborg also proffers an opinion that this large number may be characterized as genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes, Mr. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wanted to clarify for the record. This is not a report by Dr. Brunborg, this is an article that was published on 10 July 2002. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It does say in the footnote "Report," Your Honour, so we weren't trying to mislead anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no one is suggesting that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What I'd like to do --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I would like to add something. This article has been enclosed and the Prosecutor has it. I have enclosed it as one of the positions by Dr. Brunborg. I did not come across it in a piece of literature that does not exist in this Court. That's why I said "report," because I see it as one of the positions and pieces of evidence that Mr. Brunborg has published and offered to this Tribunal as part of the way he saw things that he was dealing with. I did not consider - maybe I should have - that you can have one position when writing the report for the Tribunal and a different position as part of your scientific publication, and you still write about the same thing, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. And we're not personally criticising Mr. Brunborg, as I earlier stated, but I'd like to go back to, a little bit, you had mentioned that -- you know, when we talked about the flaws and the errors that we see, really, am I correct that in essence what you're saying is that the methodology that was used fell below the acceptable, reasonable standards that demographers would utilise in making or having analyses to come up with a conclusion? Is that the essence of it, if I may?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that would be the essence. The methodology is not standardised, it's not scientific. A standard statistical method is modified and adjusted to the end result. In other words, in most statistical research or serious a demographic research will you be able to find that the standard matching procedure has 71 keys. It's non-existent. You can define your own key and say what it consists of, and you can stand by that, but within one and the same research, you define 71 different possibilities. So if something is found unsuitable to my needs, I still have an opportunity to interchange within those different keys.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'll discuss keys with you, hopefully, in a few minutes or a little later, but what I want to talk about now briefly are the sources that were utilised. You mentioned earlier today that when methodology is being utilised, the first and perhaps most important step is the choice of sources. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just put the question to you. Thank you for just recollecting that. Now, you list several sources on page 5 of your report, and just so you can follow along and others can follow along, you list the sources that Mr. Brunborg utilised and the sources that he didn't utilise that were readily available. What I'd like to know is that whether demographers, such as yourself, and statisticians, do they typically utilise these sources that are listed in conducting this type of analysis, and, secondly, because I know you're going to give longer answers, are these sources considered --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you take things one at a time or can I take them one at a time?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you qualify the sources of data, then there is something that we call a general breakup of data. They can be official and unofficial. What is the difference between the official and unofficial sources of data? When it comes to the official sources of data, such as a census, the date on mortality and so on and so forth, there is an authority behind these sources, the authority of a specialised institution or the authority of the state. At the moment, I'm not saying -- discussing the quality of these data, but the quality of a certain professional organisation does provide a guarantee that these data are at least minimally reliable. The authority of an official organisation goes even to such an extent to warn the end user about the degree of the reliability of the data, whether they are scrupulously correct or should be taken with reservations. For example, when it comes to vital statistics, when you're talking about the rates of mortality or natality, you will see some dates in brackets. This means that the end user is warned that the data in brackets is of dubious quality, and then there is an explanation: "We believe that there was a shortfall in the registration of certain facts," and so on and so forth. Behind official sources of data, there is an authority, and this authority is in charge of verifying those data. When it comes to an unofficial source of data, there may be an authority behind, but it doesn't have to be. Unofficial sources of data may be an association, an organisation, which do not deal with statistics as their primary activity, but a statistician who obtains that information will be able to turn these data into official data. For example, the Red Cross does not practice the methods and standards of methodological research, but a statistician who obtains that data is duty-bound to apply the standards and methods of the profession and turn the unofficial data into more or less reliable data. There are various unofficial sources. For example, there are unofficial sources whose authors are not known, and you also have those unofficial sources of data which are never verified or publicly announced. I've mentioned the PHR here. I may be mistaken, but I have not come across, in my work, and if I'm mistaken I apologise in advance, that a list or the source of data collected by the PHR has ever been disclosed anywhere but here in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're being infected by Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell me if it would be reasonable for a demographer and a statistician to use these sources as part of their methodology for purposes of evaluating or analysing things such as that which occurred in Srebrenica in 1995? And specifically I'm relating to the seven sources that you cite on page 5 of your report. Would it be reasonable for demographers and statisticians to utilise those sources?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the ones that he did not use? Is that what you mean, the sources that the Prosecution expert did not use? Not only would it have been reasonable, but it would have been professionally honest. Why am I saying this? A selective choice of a source of data, when you have more at your disposal than you have chosen automatically means that you are adjusting some research to what you expect to obtain as your end result. And not only is it a selective choice of data, which makes you rely on certain choices that may be of certain quality or not, and at the same time you're ignoring certain sources which are either similar or of better quality. In addition to that, if you compare several sources of data, you obtain more reliable data, and you can say with a higher degree of certainty what would be the minimally reliable figures, or you can limit yourself and say this is possible or this is probable because you have various sources of data. The more sources of data you have, the higher degree of reliability in your statistical research you may expect to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And slightly -- the next question, I think you may have covered it, but just so I'm clear and we have it clear on the record: Is the failure or refusal, with all due respect, to use these sources that you even highlighted, which are readily available, does that raise doubt as to the reliability and the validity of the OTP demographic experts and their reports in connection with the missing and dead?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally do harbour reasonable doubt. If the sources have been at your disposal since 2001 and you are using them in one case and not in the other, then I really do not have a logical explanation why you decided to use it in one case, and you know that it would provide you with good information or at least you could say, "This is what I used," but reject it for certain reasons. A statistician, a demographer, has the right to consult various sources, but ignore them, but there has to be an explanation for that. "I have consulted something, but not take it into account for certain reasons." There's no single expert opinion by Dr. Brunborg and his associate with regard to Srebrenica, and the first one was drafted in 2000 and the last one in 2005, so they have not mentioned the BH Army, the DEM 2, the MA [indiscernible], so these are not sources that were not available. They are available -- they have been available to them in the demographic department of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find, doctor, in your research and study of the reports that you evaluated for us, did you find whether Mr. Brunborg or Madam Ewa Tabeau gave any explanation or reason as to why they decided not to utilise these reasonable sources for purposes of either verification or for purposes of cross-checking to further validate their analyses and conclusions? Did they give any explanations in any of their reports as to why they didn't use these sources?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no explanation whatsoever why they didn't use them. They don't even say that they exist. However, in the material that I've seen here by Ms. Ewa Tabeau, who matched the data from the BH Army and the census of the population; i.e., the list of the missing and dead that was compiled by the Prosecutor, gives one sentence and says that this source of data is really not of high quality. This is the first time I ever saw it. I have also listened to the examination-in-chief of Dr. Brunborg, who said that in order for him -- that he would have established that there were no dead before 1995 if he had matched that with the list of fallen soldiers. In other words, I have not seen that recorded in any of the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, Doctor, would using these readily-available sources assist us in having a more complete, thorough and accurate assessment, from a demographics perspective, of determining the missing and dead?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object. This is very leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have to be very honest to my learned colleague. I've been a practitioner for over 25 years, and I've actually given lectures on leading questions and provided students with specifically what is or is not. This is in no way a leading question whatsoever. I'm asking the doctor whether she has an opinion as to whether or not these sources, which they've had in their possession, which they acknowledge are reasonable, whether or not that could assist us in getting a more thorough, complete, and accurate description of that which their demographics experts were trying to utilise. I do take offence to the issue that it's leading. I think it's not leading. I think that it's a very appropriate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think simply asking, "How would these sources be used," would be a more appropriate question and not leading at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I need to consult with my colleagues, and we'll come back to you shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ostojic, our conclusion is that this area has already been dealt with by the witness, so you can move to your next question and to specific areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: More specific than sources, Mr. President; is that what you're asking me? This area is a specific area. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but you have to be specific, in other words, and ask no leading questions on specific matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, looking at these sources, if we can stick with that for a moment, do you have an opinion as to whether or not, by reviewing these sources, they would assist us in providing a more complete, thorough, and accurate assessment of the missing and dead?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back to square one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back to square one. I mean, we avoided telling you whether we considered it a direct question, a leading question, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'll move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you could draw your attention to page 6 of your report, and I just notice in the top there you have a statement, and it was translated into English as being inadmissible. And if you just follow with me, right before the bold point. And I think, Doctor, it doesn't really have the meaning as it does in the B/C/S version, if I'm not mistaken, but I'm going to have you help us understand that, because your report is sprinkled, quite candidly, with a lot of words such as "inadmissible." Are you telling us with respect to the report that you provide that it's more of a question of reliability and validity, because I think it falls within the parlance of the Trial Chamber to determine whether something is admissible or not.
