And with the most respect to you, when you say that "the methodological errors or flaws are inadmissible," can you tell us whether -- what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, objection. What does "admissibility" mean? Is this leading to a legal conclusion? And it's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I quite frankly think there was, in the translation part, they have utilised the word "inadmissible" rather broadly, and I'm asking her to clarify. If she says that she thinks it's inadmissible, but I think we heard from her testimony and the translators today, that in fact when she utilised the same word, she was referring to reliability as well as validity, and I'm just asking her to clarify that in her report, so when the Court reviews it in English, which I presume it will review it in English, that you have a clearer picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I join that position. It was one of the few questions I was going to ask Ms. Radovanovic, and the report repeatedly uses the word, and it doesn't appear to make any sense in English. And I think it's a perfectly proper question for the Trial Chamber to have that matter clarified so they understand the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With two such distinguished lawyers disagreeing with you, you can't be right, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I respectfully disagree with that, Your Honours. They could simply ask, "How is it inadmissible," or, "What does 'admissible' mean," as opposed leading with a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have no problem here, being assumed that the word "inadmissible" could in itself be inherently confusing, they're asking for a clarification, so please go ahead, Mr. Ostojic, or, Madam, if you could answer the question, please, and clarify it for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that now we have a confused terminology. When I say "nedopustivo," it means impermissible from a methodological point of view. I use this term quite often, not only here but in scientific literature in my language. To say that something is impermissible, it means that this is improper from a methodological point of view. You simply cannot do it that way. And that's why I used this term. I wanted to be a little bit more polite. I wasn't aware of the legal implications of the discrepancy between the two terms in my language versus in the English language. So when I say "unacceptable" or "inadmissible," as it was used in the report, I'm not saying that I'm going to allow it in and then let somebody else evaluate it. When I say "nedopustivo," "impermissible," it means that it is improper, deficient in methodological terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. It helps a little, I think. Doctor, it's my understanding that a few days ago, you reviewed also some material, I think, on the 25th of July, 2008. Did you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, and I wasn't around at that time and I'm sorry for that, can you just tell us what is it that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reviewed the Prosecutor's disclosure that refers to soldiers. The Prosecutor disclosed that by matching the BiH Army base, the census and the list of missing persons on the Prosecutor's list of missing and dead, resulted in some figures, i.e., that over 70 per cent of the soldiers are on the Prosecutor's list of dead and missing. Up to the disclosure of this material, this list could have been perceived as a list that contained exclusively civilians, especially if you read previous reports; i.e., if you read what Dr. Brunborg wrote, and he wrote that those were exclusively non-combatant men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, again, I don't want to go back to sources, but that's another source that could have been utilised in connection with providing a -- without offending my colleague -- a report, I guess, as opposed to a reasonable or a reliable or a valid report, if you will? That's a source that could be used; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That is a source that has been in existence since 2001 at the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let me move on now to the next issue that I wanted to discuss with you, and that is matching as well as identification key. I know in your report, in the summary section, you discuss both of those items, matching and key. I'd like to direct our attention to page 31 of your report, where you identify -- and just so that we're clear, and I know you gave the example yesterday utilising an ATM card with the four numbers. Is using four numbers actually the key or are those four numbers an element within an identification key?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have not explained that properly. When I say "a key," every matching key consists of several elements, and a key may contain ten elements or two elements, seven, eight. There is never one single element in a key. So when it comes to the personal identification number, you have 13 elements, because there are 13 digits that make up the identification number for every citizen. When you design a matching key, you determine the elements, and that is what Dr. Brunborg says when he presents his 71 keys. The first key is the name, the father's name, the date of birth, which means that one key or one criterion contains more than one element. The more there are elements, the more possibilities that the result will be more accurate. As you exclude one element after another, you modify your key, and then you --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't mean to be rude, to interrupt you, but you're getting a little --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I apologise to the Court and to you, Doctor, for interrupting you, but you're getting just a little bit ahead of me, and I wanted to have a better appreciation for this identification key, if you will, and the elements within this key. But help us understand this: How many different keys does Dr. Brunborg utilise when presenting his analysis when looking at this material that you've shared; how many?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Brunborg provides a list of keys that he used for the matching exercise with the census. The list contains 71 keys.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's what I understood, and we'll take it one step at a time. So he has 71 different keys, and within each of those keys there are these elements that you say, such as name, last name, place of -- date of birth, if you will, or place of residence, I think as you list on page 31 of your report. What effect, if any, or what significance, if any, does utilising different identification keys in this matching process have on the ultimate result that Dr. Brunborg has given or provided to us?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The significance is major. First of all, the methodological rule says that you should not change your keys within the course of one activity process, which means if Dr. Brunborg has set up a key that consists of, for example, seven elements, the name, the last name, then father's name, the date, the month and the year of birth, and the place of residence, he should have used that key to do the matching of all the sources of data, which means I have a list, I have seven elements for one key, and then I run the seven elements through the census. And in order for something to be matched with something else, or, rather, for something to be identified, there should be an absolute match between the name, the last name, the father's name, the date of birth, the place of residence. So there should be an absolute match. After this is completed, you end up with data, and you can say with confidence, "I have found 500, but I'm not happy with that, it's too little," so I reduce the key by one element and I say, "I am looking for an identical name, the date of birth," but I have changed the key because I have omitted something from the key, such as the place of residence. Then I run that key through the census, and then I have a perfect match for a thousand people, for example. And then I do say, "Well, it's not enough," and then I reduce the key by another element and I say, "I want the name, the last name, the father's name, but I don't want the date of birth, I just want the month and the year of birth." And again I repeat the exercise. I'm just doing this for academic exercise. And finally I end up with 3.000 identical names. Again, I'm not happy, so I reduce the key by the element of the date of birth, I just reduce it to the name. I end up with 4.000. I'm still not happy. I can't give you that for all the 71 keys, but finally end up with the initial of the first name, the father's name, and the year of birth, and I end up with, let's say, 5.000 matches according to a certain criteria. I don't know whether it is criterion 40, 41, or 42, where Dr. Brunborg sets up, as his criteria, the initial and the year of birth plus/minus five years. He can then end up with everybody with initial "S", the last name "Radovanovic," who was born in the year 1949, plus/minus five years, which means that person may have been born any time between the year 1994 and 1999, and when he gets matches based on that criteria, he will then apply the so-called visual method, and he can end up with thousands upon thousands of such cases. I believe that according to the Rule 40, he could have ended up with over 100.000 such cases. Then you do the eliminating exercise and you end up with 6.000 or 7.000, because what you do, you do a visual exercise. You're looking for elements that suit you, that suit your end result, which means you can be very subjective in determining what you want to end up with; i.e., you can open a space to your decision being more decisive and more relevant than the appropriate key or the objective findings. If you want an objective finding, you have to have an objective source of data and an objective key. Every expert, every professional, can set up a more relaxed or more strict key. A more relaxed key will make your end result less reliable. And this is what I said yesterday, but I may not have been clear enough. Had Dr. Brunborg provided any statistics in any of his reports and stated: "I used 71," five, whatever keys, and then indicated the first key that contains such-and-such elements, "I managed to match 10 per cent. Using the second key that contains such-and-such element, I matched 30 per cent, the fifth," and so on, if he had given us an overview of how keys were used, and what keys were used, and the possibility of matching, then we could assess the reliability of the match that he obtained. We could see the combinatorics of it in the combination of those keys, and combinatorics of course affects the reliability of the results.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think you just said, in essence, among many other things, that the more relaxed key, the less reliable. In this -- in your evaluation and review of the materials from Dr. Brunborg and others, did you find that there were -- there was this more relaxed key or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. This has been asked and answered over the last day and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, I'll move on because I'm going to get to this point eventually, but I thought I'd short-circuit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you look at these relaxed keys, you'd have to look at each element, would you not, as we discussed and as reflected in your report on page 31, by utilising -- let's take it one step further so that -- or actually the essence of it. If you utilise different elements and many different elements, that creates a situation -- or you tell me, does that create a more relaxed or more stringent key for purposes of reliability and/or validity?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you don't have numerical indicators, such as the personal ID number, which is a reliable key, but if you provide the elements of a key for some person, then the more elements, the more certain you are that the datum is reliable. If someone is looking for Svetlana Radovanovic in the Bosnia-Herzegovina census results, I gave that as an example yesterday, and if the key is "Svetlana, father's name, last name Radovanovic," such-and-such date of birth, month of birth, year of birth, place of birth, permanent residence, then the probability that the person identified as Svetlana Radovanovic will be the one you're looking for will be greater. If somebody asks you to look for Svetlana Radovanovic, who may have been born between '44 and '54, the probability that the reliability of the datum that you obtain is going to be reliable is very low. And there is always this possibility that the person does the matching decides whether it is matched or not. The matching is highly dubious, the moment you introduce the element of subjectivity. I tried to explain that. Perhaps I wasn't really successful in it. But would any of us agree, when taking money out of the bank machine, to -- not to know the PIN but to just use any random selection of numbers? In that case, nobody would keep their money in the bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic and Dr. Radovanovic, we have a feeling that the testimony, and that includes the questions as well, is becoming too repetitive, so if you could avoid putting questions to the witness which, if answered, can only be repetitive, please, both of you, try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, in your field of study and in demographics, in creating these identification keys while performing this type of analysis, do demographers typically look for uniformity and standardised and/or fixed elements in order to create this identification key?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, in the field of demographics, what do experts such as yourself look for or what is necessary in order to maintain some level of objectivity in creating these elements and identification keys?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The matching method is used in statistics. It has been used for a long time in statistics, particularly when you have a census and when you want to match the population, households, things like that. In this kind of research of the type done by Dr. Brunborg, individual data have never been used, ever, in order to present something in this manner, so this is not controversial in statistics. You have a code, you say, "Look for 1287 and 12." In every questionnaire, you have those codes, so you never ask for -- look -- you never say, "Look for such-and-such a person by name." In scientific statistician-type research, you don't have this kind of thing. In demographic research, this is the first time that somebody did this kind of research, comparing individual data through several data sources, using such keys.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But let me just move on to another topic, in the interests of time, and maybe we won't -- and I think we understand it a little bit better, and thank you for that. I want to direct your attention back to subparagraph (h) in your report on page 8 in English, where you talk about a failure to discount, and you talk about the fictitious names that appear and all that. I really didn't understand that fully, and with all due respect, Doctor, it says, and I'll read it, although we can all read it there: "It is methodologically inadmissible to fail -- to discount from the study all persons for whom there are reasonable grounds to suspect that they are fictitious." And not to ask you a leading question, but why, why do you hold that opinion? Like why would it be impermissible or inadmissible, if you will?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you have a methodological requirement to the fact that in order to prove that a person exists, I have to verify that person's existence in the 1991 census by identifying that person through a matching procedure, if this is one of the requirements for the proof of the existence of an individual, and then if you prove by matching that 87 per cent of persons were identified through this matching process -- now, I'm not even going into whether the key is good or bad, whether there was 71 criteria or whatever, but you prove that 87 of those persons existed, that means that in your research you managed to prove that 13 per cent of these people does not exist in accordance with the results of your research. It would be professionally proper to exclude them and to say, "Okay, I'm going to work with this sample of people I have proven exist." But Dr. Brunborg does not do that. He says, "I fail to find the 13 per cent, but I distributed them around." So you don't know if this person exists, because they are not in the census, how can you then put them in Srebrenica, how do you know that they are Muslims or Bosniaks? Mr. Brunborg, in his tables, in his reports, shows that he has 999 persons whose ethnic background is unknown to him, 999 people whose ethnic background you don't know, and you take them from the census, so you don't even know where they live or where they were at the time. I apologise, I'm really getting into the stride.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's very interesting, as am I as well, and thank you and I apologise. And what I really want to know, Doctor, is: What effect, if any, does this have, the failure to discount, in your opinion, of course, with respect to the overall report and the conclusions that were rendered by Dr. Brunborg; what affect does it have?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it should have significant impact on the end results.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know, but share with us what effect, in your opinion, it has on the overall results. I understand that it's significant, but just share with us what impact that you believe that it has.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the results are significantly increased, and there is statistical evidence. I'm not even going into whether the figure is correct or incorrect. I don't know what the figure is for the victims. But using an erroneous methodological number, you increase the certain statistical mass knowingly, because if you increase the statistical mass, you automatically increase other relative indicators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me just maybe -- I think it's related, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- I think it's related, but can you tell me what a "empty field" is or "empty fields"? And you mentioned it yesterday in your testimony on page 81, lines 15 through 21, I believe. Just explain that concept to me, and then I have a couple of questions in connection with that, "empty fields."

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Empty fields have to do with the quality of data sources. Here, I tried to agree -- or, rather, I agree with Dr. Brunborg, when he lists three key reasons determining the quality of the data sources. The first is the problem of coverage. If I don't know the area covered or included, then I can include or exclude whatever I want. The second problem is the data that exists, but are incorrect. What does it mean? If you have a questionnaire or if you have datum, first name, last name, but you don't have the date of birth, "date of birth," then, is an empty field. Or if you have an existing datum, for instance, first name, last name, father's name, and the date of birth is wrong, it indicates that somebody was born on the 1st of January, 1949, whereas the actual date of birth is the 10th of May, 1952, so the empty field is -- indicates that there is no information. You remember that we made this comparison with the soldiers and using just a year of birth or the full date, or when we said that the Red Cross and the Brunborg list does not contain 35 -- that 35 entries -- 35 per cent of the entries do not have date of birth indicated, these are the empty fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said this goes more to the qualitativeness as opposed to the quantitativeness of the report, but is it significant or what is the significance if you have an increase in the number of empty fields within the demographic study and/or statistical study, if any?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is highly significant. If you don't have a datum, how can you match information? How would Dr. Brunborg match 70 per cent of the people using very strict keys? In his -- among his data, he has 35 per cent of entries that do not have date of birth listed, so it automatically lowers the quality of the data, of the results. And how can Dr. Brunborg decide who was killed after the 10th of July, 1995, if for 35 per cent of the entries he does not have the date? Were these people killed on the 1st of July, the 2nd of July, the 3rd? Dr. Brunborg sets the 10th as his limit, so all the people in his list that do not have the date of disappearance entered, how are they distributed in the graphs or when he has a day-by-day breakdown. Dr. Brunborg does not show information for people who were killed up until the 10th of July. It is impossible to have it because it's not on the list, it's not on the Red Cross list. How does Dr. Brunborg then put these people among those who were killed in relation to the events in Srebrenica from 11 July onwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What effect, if any, Doctor, does this have -- the qualitativeness aspect of these empty fields, as you described them in detail, what effect does it have, in your opinion as a demographer, on the reliability of such conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is extremely significant, because the results you obtain are not even minimally reliable. So it has a major influence on the reliability of the results.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Because they translate the -- what about the validity of the results? Do you have an opinion as to what affect does that qualitativeness that we were discussing with respect to the empty fields, what affect does it have on the validity of the conclusions that were reached, if any?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it affects the validity of the way in which conclusions are drawn. You make conclusions on the basis of statistical indicators that you obtained. If you obtained deficient or unreliable statistical indicators, well, then you can't draw any reliable conclusions or scrupulously correct conclusions, so it is very important. Because of the quality of the sources, because of deficient methodology, you obtain deficient statistical -- deficient statistical base, I don't know how you can expect to draw reliable conclusions about what you are considering.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I'm moving on, if I may, and I'm just directing your attention to this, as opposed to leading you into this part, and that would be to the issue of locality and a municipality. You touched on it briefly today, but I'd like, for our purposes, that you walk me through two tables from Dr. Brunborg, and the first table is table 1 from his 2003 report, which I believe is identified on my learned friend's 65 ter list as P2410. And the Court will duly note, as I'm sure my learned friends have, it does state on that exhibit that it's a 2004 report, but in looking for it, it's actually a 2003 report, April of 2003. So can we please have table 1. And then next to that, Doctor, as you're following along with me, can we have the report from Mr. Brunborg, table 6, but the report P2413, which is the November 16, 2005 report; table 6 of that report. Let me just repeat it. I would like to have, first of all, from the 2003 report, table number 1. That number, 65 ter number, is P2410. And I'd also, if possible, like to compare that table 1 from this 2003 report with table 6, again Brunborg's report of November 2005? Are you following me, at least, Doctor, and when we get it, we'll look at it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Provide us with a page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's towards the end, and it's page number 22 of the November 2005 report, so Exhibit P2413, which is table 6, is on page 22, and specifically the page number for table 1 of the 2003 report appears on page -- it's the second page, but I don't believe that they are numbered, actually. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going to ask you --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, no, and I want you to read it, but just tell me first: What is this table 1 that appears in Dr. Brunborg's 2003 report? Just give us an overview of what it is.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 2003 report, Dr. Brunborg sets up a list of the missing and dead that contains 7.433 entries. Using the same methodology that was used in 2005, he takes the 7.433 persons and distributes them into municipalities of residence, because on the basis of the census he was able to determine that this is where they lived, resided. Again, the same percentage of matches, 87 per cent, both in 2003 and 2005. The point of this table is in the fact that Dr. Brunborg distributes them not only in the five municipalities that are considered by him to be Srebrenica in the 2005 report, but you will see a column here where it says "other municipalities" in this table. This indicates that Srebrenica comprises these five municipalities and some other municipalities. In the 2005 report, there is no --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that's reflected on the screen under table 6; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to follow up --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. So the table 1 from 2003 has a note indicating that 13 per cent of the persons have not been matched, but please bear in mind that all the persons are distributed, broken down, 100 per cent, regardless of the 13 per cent that was not matched. Table 6 is the mirror image of this table, but with a twist that's presented by Dr. Brunborg in his 2005 report. Here, Dr. Brunborg does not show the breakdown municipality by municipality, municipality of residence, but place of disappearance. Let me just note here the table 1 from 2003 should be the breakdown according to place of residence, whereas table 6 from 2005 is broken down into accordance with the place of disappearance. There are 14 sites, locations, listed here. If you look at them, they are in five municipalities; Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, Zvornik, Han Pijesak. Dr. Brunborg says that the Prosecution has provided them with those locations, but those same locations are also listed in the ICRC list. But the ICRC list states both the location and the municipality where this location is. So if you have "Potocari," it says "Potocari-Srebrenica, Kravica-Bratunac," and so on. Those fourteen [as interpreted] locations cover six -- or, rather, five municipalities that Dr. Brunborg lists, Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, Zvornik, Han Pijesak, but Dr. Brunborg does not say, and here he says the total for those -- for these -- for the localities is 4.880 persons, but if you add up all of it, the total is 7.661. What is the point of this table? There are some figures, amounting to about 540 - we can find them below the total - for some locations that are not in those municipalities, so instead of listing other municipalities or other locations, Dr. Brunborg says: "Dead and missing, less than 50." That's less than 50 per location, per site. And these are locations or sites that cannot be classified in any of the five municipalities using other criteria such as, we're talking about Valjevo -- I have to read because I can't recall all the municipalities, Loznica, Rogatica, for instance, Bijeljina. These are not locations that could be put in there, on any logic, except for the fact that in those locations he encountered cases where people died between July and the end of the year 1995, so this was the criterion for putting these people -- including them on the list. Yet another location is Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting, but I just want to make clear for the record that table 1 is representing missing men by municipality of residence, per census 1991, while table 2 is representing number of Srebrenica-related missing by place of disappearance, just for clarity of record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What affect --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. That's precisely what I said, and you can read it in the record. I said that the 1991 table is by place of residence and the 2005 is by location of disappearance, place of disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, what affect does any, doing it that way, and you said that there is a -- he puts plus or minus 50 or greater than -- strike that, he didn't say plus or minus. You say he lists, as we can see on the table, greater than 50 or less than 50, and I know you've stated you found 540 or so individuals that do not belong within that grouping. What affect does it have on his overall conclusions, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, Dr. Brunborg really wanted, at any cost, to find as many missing and dead as possible, and it does have an impact because it significantly increases the number. But methodologically speaking, it is quite impossible to do that, if you are doing your job properly, lege artis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Doctor, with the highest of respect to you, we're not looking for the motivations behind Dr. Brunborg. My question was straightforward, and I think you answered it, but just so that we're clear: The significance of doing it when you do these localities and municipalities, as we've seen in table 1 and table 6 of his 2003 and 2005 reports respectively, is there is an increase in the conclusions, or what affect does it have on the conclusions, an increase or a decrease? That's the number of men missing and/or dead.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll have to admit that I don't understand your question. Increase or decrease of a certain mass has to impact everything, but the only question is whether you reached a number by methodologically improper means. If you had applied the correct methodology, then you would have ruled out all the increases that you have here. That is the basic problem with this. So if you had applied the rules -- the professional standards, you would have not have obtained the results that you obtained. So failure to apply -- failure to comply with the professional standards in your field leads to something that is, professionally speaking and methodologically speaking, proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And let me turn to a different topic and a different subject, if I may. If we could look at P515, please, and I have a question because there's been some evidence in connection with this. And since you deal with mortality and morbidity and demographics and statistics, I wanted to direct your attention specifically to paragraph 6 of P515, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, page 70, line 18, it should read "is not proper."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, it's time for the lunch break, so we can stop here, and you can start with your new chapter after lunch one hour from now. So we'll start at 10 to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good afternoon, everybody. Yes, Mr. Ostojic. I saw you standing. Is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No. I thought, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just didn't know if you had anything else --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw you standing, then I saw you sit down, and then I saw Mr. Nikolic switch on his microphone, so I didn't know what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It was just, I wasn't sure if you had something else to say, so I didn't want to stand up. I was trying to be polite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I better keep my mouth shut.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, if we can just proceed, I asked just before the break for us to look at Exhibit P515, and I think it should be up on the e-court or the screen before you. And specifically I'm directing your attention to paragraph number 6 of this exhibit, and it discusses, actually, what seems to be someone reporting the birth rate on a given day in 1995, namely, the 13th or 12th of July, 1995. And my question to you, although it's somewhat related, the significance, given you're a demographer and we're talking about statistics, have you encountered in your years of experience and profession that 50 babies were delivered on one given day in that region or in that area?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I have to intervene along the professional line. I -- and the translation I received was "the birth rate," but it's a different thing. The birth rate is the frequency of birth with respect to a certain population, and if it was said the natality rate was three per mil, then I would note that three babies were born in a population of 1.000. Here we're talking about the number of babies who were born on the 13th of July, and the number was 50. I wouldn't be able to tell you whether this is okay or not. At this moment, I think that the number is exaggerated, because there is no single data speaking about previous numbers of babies born on one day, so the figure of 50 on the 13th of July, without an insight into some other information as to how many women, how many of them fertile, I wouldn't be able to tell you. I can't tell you with any degree of certainty or reliability. It seems, according to some information about births, which is not very reliable in large areas with a high number of population, it is possible that 50 may be born in one day, but I'm not even sure whether 50 were born on that one day, on the 13th of July. So I wouldn't be able to give you any reliable assessment. In my view, this seems like an exaggerated number, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that, and I just raised it as a point, and I apologise maybe for even asking you that. Let me ask you if we can direct your attention to your report again, 3D398, specifically page 22, and I wanted to just go over the table 3 that you discussed with my learned friend, Madam Nikolic, because I'm not sure I understood what you're trying to show us here. And this involves, obviously, the DET or DEM 2T, which is the database of deaths for 1992 and 1995. Now, you've given us a couple of examples, and I know we looked at one of them, but I wanted to look at the other three that you've highlighted for us here. First tell us briefly what this table represents, and what is the point of it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The table 3? This is just an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's catch up, Doctor. Thank you. It's, I think, on page 20, in the B/C/S, and on page 22 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an example how the data-matching exercise between the sources DEM 2T and the list of missing and dead offered by the Prosecutor's office, may result in the identical overlapping of first names, last names, the dates of birth, or the years of birth, but offering some different data. To say the least, this is just a good indication, indicating the reliability of data, to say whether individuals 2, 3, or 4, who have identical data in the Prosecutor's list and the DEM 2T, but with different dates of death and different places of death. If, on the one hand, you have the source of data compiled by the statisticians and, on the other hand, a source of data relying on erroneous reports, then we have to question the reliability of the data that we obtain, i.e., we have to ask ourselves whether there are some other people on the Prosecutor's list that may be qualified as fictitious.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know you highlighted those before, but I need -- for more precision or to be more precise, would that be, the fact that you think it's unreliable, goes to the methodology that's used, or is that the lack of using all the sources or a more complete set of sources, or does it go directly towards the analysis that the demographer to utilised when they these people, for example, based on the Prosecution's estimate as to date of death within their demographic studies?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did the matching exercise, and the Prosecutor's experts never used the DEM 2 database. I'm trying to explain how a selective choice of data may influence the quality of the data obtained by the Prosecutor's experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And certainly for our case, because we're dealing with Srebrenica, you highlighted two, I think, specific instances in which you found through the DEM 2T database, that these two individuals, when you look specifically at either the identification key or the elements within the identification key, you found that their date of death preceded, and in one instance two years, the events that unfolded July 1995 in Srebrenica; is that basically what you're trying to show here?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have an example. When you do the matching exercise between the Prosecutor's list and the identified persons, and you will find that in tables, whose number I know at the moment [as interpreted], you will find the cases of a mismatch, although the Prosecutor takes them as being identified, although they involve different dates. I'm talking about tables 1 and 2 in my report. So there is a match between the dates, the names, last name, and the father's name, but there is no match between the dates of birth. The Prosecutor says that they have identified or matched, as identified dead bodies, even cases like this. Table 1 says these are people on the Prosecutor's list, and, for example, the name, the last name, the father's name on the Prosecutor's list bears the date of birth "8 February 1957," and has an ID number which was adopted from the ICRC database. In the list of identified dead persons, the same person, i.e., the person with the same name, last name, father's name, and the same BAZ identification provided by the ICRC, shows a completely different date of birth. Now, the question arises whether these two persons are one and the same, and if the Prosecutor says that they have had a match, then one of these persons is fictitious. If your match is based on a different list of persons and accepted that that was the correct date of birth, then I don't understand the facts that you rely on to provide the date of birth 11 September 1955 rather than 8 February 1957. What happens then with the people who appear under the same ID as in the first list? What the Prosecutor does, they leave them in the list as if they really existed, and then they feature in that list both as the dead person and as the missing person. The correct procedure would be this: If you identify somebody and then you find another better match, then you have to eliminate the first person from your first list. That would be the correct procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. And let me ask you this so that we can all get a better appreciation for how we would do this matching: Can you give us an idea of when you did this DEM 2T match with the other data as you've highlighted in your report with these four samples, can you tell us how extensive that project is to do that type of matching, if at all?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you use the correct key, then the process lasts for as long as you are able to apply all the elements. For example, you take a key in order to match people from one list to another list, and if you're asking me about the time frame, it would take a certain time, but only if your databases are in order. I have looked at DEM 2T. I have not analysed its quality, I have not controlled its quality. Within half an hour or one hour, I have -- I was able to obtain results from which I singled out these particular examples as typical and characteristic. Seven days was just not enough for me to check all the possibilities and all the variations that are possible, but I still wanted to take something reliable to show all the things that exist. My time was rather limited, and I could not embark on the most detailed and most reliable analysis. I am just showing you the inconsistencies that exist, and I'm also trying to indicate everything that may have an influence on the acceptability and permissibility of data, starting with the source to the matching procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I just have a couple more question, but just to follow up on your answer here: When you talk about correctness, and I'm not sure if it's a translation issue or not, but when you say they have to use the correct key, and I apologise for having to lead on this issue but I think it's important, are you saying that the identification keys and is in its elements, within it, that they have to be uniform or do you think they do not have to be uniform, or standardised or not standardised, because I don't know what you mean when you say "correct"?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Correct" means that after the matching exercise, you will end up with a degree of reliability of the data you have obtained. Maybe I'm not able to give you a precise explanation. A degree of reliability is based on the fact that I have several elements that allow me to state that the person was X/Y, but if I only have the name, the date of birth, and the father's name, the reliability or the probability that you have obtained the right match decreases. The more elements I have in a key, the better -- the more likelihood that your data will be more reliable, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you find, in the reports from the demographers that the OTP put forth, that there was a uniformity in the identification keys that were utilised, or matching?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can you talk about uniformity if you have 71 keys?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And let me just put the next -- and I understand, and I just wanted to get a better appreciation for it. Thank you. In looking at this table 3, and I admittedly -- as you've acknowledged, you've done a short amount of time on it or did not have sufficient time to look at it, can you tell us, based upon a reasonable degree of certainty, what the significance is of your findings in connection with this DEM 2T report, and considering that you've done this match?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you with a high degree of certainty that the DEM 2T base would have contributed to a high reliability of the results, whether there are only 4 or maybe 40 or 400 or 4.000 cases in this base, at this moment, I can't tell you. However, the cases that I have analysed without any specific control, without any specific key, just adopting what the Prosecutor says, show that the use of this base would have contributed to a higher reliability of results. It would be only if I were able to control the whole base, if I had ample of time at my disposal, that I could say that the DEM 2T base should be rejected because a matching exercise with the Prosecutor's list does not give significant results that might have an influence on the Prosecutor's list. It would be only then that I would be able to say that the base should be rejected. Before that, I'm not able to say whether this source of information is good or not. I only know that this database is official. And if this database is official, then I would have to take it into account when I controlled my own results; i.e., the rest of the results compiled by the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and I think I'm near the end. You talked about reliability and in utilising these types of sources. Can you tell us if you have an opinion as to whether or not utilising these types of sources would assist us in looking at these matchings and ultimately determining the missing and the dead, as to the accuracy and the thoroughness? Would it assist us in that vein as well?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it would. It is not just the inclusion of certain sources of data that matters. It is also the exclusion. So if I have a higher number of databases made besides 615, and if each of these source of data is controlled by me, then I can say this one will be rejected for a good reason and the other one will be adopted. And then this would be a good-enough guarantee that I will achieve a higher degree of reliability in my results. If I concentrate in advance only on those sources of data that I have used since 2000 and that have yielded certain results, and I'm not interested in any other source of data, I don't think that the approach is really good, and you cannot say with any degree of certainty that your results are reliable. All the sources of data that I have used point to the fact that the reliability of the results obtained by the Prosecutor would have been much higher if they had used other bases, and they would have dispelled various myths or errors, the error about the number of people before the event, their status, and many other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would examining those types of sources, and specifically the one we're discussing, would that also assist us for purposes of completeness?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusions would be more reliable and more significant, in qualitative terms. The Prosecutor's experts had only quantity in mind. In any demographic research, what matters is also quality, not just quantity. Quantity does not have to bear witness to the quality, but if you have certain structures, then you have certain information about the quality of the population. If you have the status of certain individuals, that is also quality, but you don't show that. We don't have the whole picture. Not only do we not have the whole picture, but we have a problem highlighted only from one side, and that's where the problem arises from.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, and I'm done with my questions. And thank you, Mr. President, for allowing me if I've gone over the estimate of an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll wait for Mr. Ostojic to sit down so that we can see one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon, Dr. Radovanovic. It's --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- sometime since we last saw one another. I've got a few questions for you, I think, on topics you haven't been asked about before, and I'd like to ask by asking you about the 1991 census. That was a census that was conducted before the war began in Bosnia and Herzegovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you help us as to the time frame over which the information that produced that census was gathered?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, there was a census every ten years. There were long preparations preceding every census, but there's also a law regulating the methodology, the instruments, and when I say "instruments," I mean the forms, and also the duration of every census, how many days. Also, it prescribes the critical moment. It also prescribes the time needed for the analysis of all the collected data, how much time you have to produce tables, how much time you have before you publish the results. In other words, there is a schedule that has to be complied with. The 1991 census, in technical terms, complied with the prescribed deadlines, although there was a quite an unsettlement in the air at the time. The processes of data did not comply with the deadlines, as far as I know. The first results at the level of the Federation of Yugoslavia were published within a month and a half to two months. The first -- the initial results imply that all the former republics had to submit to the-then Federal Bureau of Statistics of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, certain information that had been collected by the census which had to do with the total number of population, and at that moment also the national breakdown, the total number of household. At that time, the census also took into account farming households and a certain head-of-cattle information. These initial results had to be submitted by all the former republics of Yugoslavia to the former federal Bureau of Statistics. As for the final results, they are a different thing. Unlike the initial results, the final results are much more elaborate. They don't show just the numbers of population, but also the structures of population. They break down population according to certain characteristics and attributes, and they also show information in a layered form, starting with the settlement to the republic and the state. The processing of all the material collected in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as far as I know, because of the situation that prevailed at the moment because of the war, did not follow the prescribed routine, and the first book as a result of the census, the first analysis that had been carried out in Zagreb in Croatia, was published only in 1995. That first book, that that -- the first statistical book contains the total number of population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, broken down by ethnic affiliation, starting with the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina, all its municipalities, all the settlements within the municipalities of the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you for that very complete answer, and you've pre-empted my next question, which is that the information in the census of 1991 covers all municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina and all ethnic groups; doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to say something about that. In statistics, there is something which was complied with in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia, the so-called broad national classification and the narrow national classification. Both may be applied when publishing data. Sometimes it is pointless to publish data according to the broad national classification. We were an ethnically heterogenous country which had a number of ethnic groups and communities that were all concentrated predominantly in one republic and did not exist in another, for example, the so-called Sokci, or at least their majority, reside in Vojvodina. However, the broad national classification for the whole of Yugoslavia covers everything, so Croatia did not publish their data according to the national criteria with the element Sokci. That doesn't exist. After the broad national classification, there is something known as narrow national classification, so that the census in Bosnia-Herzegovina comprised only Serbs, Croats, Bosniaks, Yugoslavs, and as far as I can remember, other nationalities and non-applicable or unknown. Amongst other nationalities or non-applicable, there is other ethnic communities that declared their national status in the census. They could have said that they were either Roma, Jews, English, Polish, but when the results are published in statistical books, you cannot find that broad national classification. Most probably there is a census on magnetic media where you can obtain statistical data applying also that broader national classification, not just the narrow one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you again for that. Now, the principal purpose in using the 1991 census as a point of reference by Mr. Brunborg is, effectively, to establish that people on missing persons lists were real people; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask you, please, about your observations in relation to the 1991 census, firstly in relation to its reliability as a source of data about persons.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I believe that the census of Bosnia and Herzegovina was successful. But what does it mean? It means that you cannot apply the same assessment to all the characteristics. There are some characteristics or attributes which were obtained based on subjective criteria. Nationality is a subjective criterion. In one census, I can declare myself as a Serb, in another one as a Yugoslav, and a third one as a -- a national [indiscernible], so I have the right to declare myself differently with respect to my nationality. All these questions that rely on a subjective criterion may always be disputed. Questions that have an objective element to it; for example, where I was born, what schools I completed, cannot be disputed. They are very reliable. However, the 1991 census is specific in some other terms. It is not specific in terms of the questions in the questionnaire and not in terms of the quality of the data obtained as a result of these questions. The 1991 census is the only census which, because of the way it was processed, that was scanning, bears the first name, the last name, the father's name. These data are not census data. They are never checked, and they had never been entered in the system. It was done for the first time in 1991. So when you're talking about the first and the last names and the father's name of a person, as the data in the census, this is erroneous. This is not something that was checked by statistical methods, because it is simply impossible. The first and the last names are technical, random entries that found themselves there because of the scanning process that was applied. If you look at all the censuses and the way they were processed at any of the republics of the former Yugoslavia before the war and after the war, because after the war, save for Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo and Metohija, all the former republics of today's state had carried out their censuses. Before 1991 and after 1991, you cannot find a single census material that would contain the first and the last names. An individual piece of information in statistics, it is protected by the law of statistics. In other words, statistics only deals in mass phenomena. I, as an individual, do not represent anything in a census. I'm just one of the individuals that feeds her own characteristics, such as date of birth, sex, education, into the collective body of population, and based on that the picture of the overall population will be obtained with me as one of its members. That is why you can say the population of Holland is so-and-so, the share of young is so-and-so, the average age is so-and-so. An individual does not exist, because statistics is not interested in individual characteristics, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And just moving slightly on from that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I'm afraid I came a little late, but I just found this answer to be totally non-responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I would suggest that you try to avoid, Professor, as well answering at this much length. I think you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll interject at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm trying my best, Dr. Radovanovic, to ask you questions that really should lead you to give fairly short answers. Because you are technically my witness, if I put words into your mouth, Ms. Soljan doubtless jump up and object, but I'm really not looking for long explanations at this point in time. So let's try another one and see how we go on. Did the 1991 census experience any difficulties in terms of the accuracy of its recorded detail?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a question it's impossible to answer clearly, or, rather, it's impossible to give a short answer. I can give a clear answer. I misspoke. If an official institution processes everything according to standard procedure, from gathering to encoding, to verification, to publishment [as interpreted], and nobody contests the data, and the institution itself does not express any doubt, then there's no difficulty. Whether we like it or not, this is official information about the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as such we have to accept it. Of course, as I've said already, certain issues can be challenged, but the census, as such, I don't believe has been challenged by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I can jog you as to which direction I'm going. Were names, both surnames and forenames, in the 1991 census recorded in both Cyrillic and Latin?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But let me underline, I don't think I explained it very well again, the name, surname, and father's name are not statistical information, and nobody ever checked it but in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. This is non-responsive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm not -- I'm not quite sure what that means. Ms. Soljan has the right to cross-examine this witness. She can object to questions I ask. I'm not sure she's entitled to object to a witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, we stopped the witness halfway through. I don't know what she was going to state. So, please, Dr. Radovanovic, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't quite finish my answer. I just wanted to remind you that this is not information that statistics checked, and it is common knowledge that in Bosnia two scripts were used. I believe they are still used today, the Latinic script, the Roman script, and Cyrillic. Both were official. It depended on the census employees. Some information was written in Cyrillic. Other information was written in Roman script. Nobody ever checked the accuracy of the writing of the registration of these names. This is the first time I'm hearing that some names were corrected here in The Hague. Correcting the spelling of names is rather a complex thing. It could be done perhaps using the machine. We have lots of letters with diacritics, "ce," "ze," "se," and others. It is possible to do it with a machine, but I don't really think so. And if you look at typed or printed texts, some letters are missing. Dr. Brunborg says that the spelling of names was corrected -- was done with the assistance of experts who are familiar with names and surnames from that region. I have certain reservations. I believe that anyone who lived in the region could proclaim themselves to be experts in our names and surnames. But to what extent it's possible to correct them, to correct the spelling, I really doubt that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is non-responsive. The simple question was whether it was Latin or Cyrillic alphabet that the 1991 census was written in. This has gone way beyond the question that was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, but it's answered the next question I was going to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So perhaps you can put again the question that hasn't been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is it your understanding that, as it were, the state of the census record made a proper understanding of what had been recorded as people's names difficult, for example, for the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could not answer the question this way, but what I know for a fact is that in the instructions of OSCE for enrolling voters for elections, there is a comment: "In view of the low quality of name registration from the previous census, it's enough to give the first three letters." And this instruction was given because all the voters who wanted to register themselves for elections had to say where they lived in 1991, and then the interviewer, to make his life easier, took a list of population, with names and surnames, but had huge problems locating the names spelled correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going to move on, as it were, from the state of the census as a record of names, and move on to its status as a means of comparison with missing persons lists. I think it's right that you have used information available -- made available to you by the Office of the Prosecution to calculate how many people had died in Bosnia and Herzegovina between 1992 and 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll put it more simply. According to your understanding, how many people died in Bosnia and Herzegovina between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are official statistics commissioned by the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY. The source of DEM 2T, done by the statistics of the Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, speak of 140.000 persons who died between 1992 and 1995. If you want me, I can look it up and see how many died of natural causes, how many died a violent death. But, in any case, this is the figure that official statistical services have produced at the request of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Radovanovic. And is it your understanding that the comparison of missing persons lists with the census of 1991 was made without the removal of the names of any of those persons, however they died?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that source was not purified from this segment. The information from 1991 was treated as if all these people still existed. If, from 1991 until 10 July 1995, somebody died, that source was not revised to exclude the deceased. They were all taken and treated as people who still existed in 1995, although some had died before 1995, some had moved away. All that population from 1991 was regarded as if nothing had changed in the meantime, those sources, those databases, were not revised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the next question is similar, but rather different, and that is: Is it your understanding that the comparison of the missing persons list relating to Srebrenica was made against the whole census information, i.e., all the people who were recorded there as living in the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Dr. Brunborg says he did that relative to Eastern Bosnia, without defining, really, what he meant by "Eastern Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you again. Now, I want to move away from the census of 1991 and move very briefly to a topic about which you have been asked quite a lot of questions. And I hope this is sufficiently novel. You've mentioned the 71 keys used by the Prosecution demographers in determining whether a match could be found between persons on missing persons lists and, for example, the census. Without going through all of them, and I think you mentioned key 42 earlier on, I wonder if you could just detail for us which of the keys you found to be, as it were, the lowest common denominator, as it were, the least points of reference used to declare a match.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the degree of reliability, I mentioned that the more elements in the key, the greater reliability. Personally, I think that in view of the possibilities provided by various sources, relative reliability would also be gained by matching names, surname, father's name, date of birth, et cetera. I'm saying "probably," meaning that the likelihood that you are meeting at least minimal standards that would produce reliable results increases, and I would accept additional sources. I'm saying "minimal," because using such a key with such a great number of elements is not possible to use with all the sources. Of course, you can put in just the name and the year of birth, but then it would be professionally proper to say "the elements of the key are the following." The likelihood of accurate findings is greater in the first case than in the second case, so you should provide two possibilities, although statistically speaking, according to the rules, you use one identification key and you do not change that key throughout the study.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that we're clear, were there keys used in establishing matches by Mr. Brunborg and his team that didn't, in fact, require knowledge of anything more than an initial of the missing person's name and surname?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had mentioned it, but again maybe I have failed to explain it properly. Dr. Brunborg offers a list of criteria or, if you wish, keys that he uses to make matches with the list of population. On that list, there are 71 keys, each containing different elements. I don't know them all by heart, but some keys start with full name, full surname, full father's name, full date of birth, et cetera. And as the number of keys increases, certain elements are either excluded or they are reduced to initial. I can't remember now whether it's the 40th or the 41st key, but it reads an initial will suffice, an initial of the first name, an initial of the surname, an initial of the father's name, et cetera. Then there's another key that says initials are allowed, the year of birth, plus/minus five. So each of the keys contains a differing number of elements. Not only are the elements different, but they can be modified. "Name" can be represented by an initial. "Year" can be year -- the year plus/minus five. I'm not saying all the keys are like that, but there are certain keys like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as to the so-called visual test, was there any protocol as to how a member of the team established a match by the visual test?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A member of the team, like me, for instance -- which member of the team do you mean? Do you mean that was I able to check how much was ascertained by the visual method?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you whether you could establish whether, within Dr. Brunborg's team, there was any protocol to establishing a visual match or whether it was simply a matter of discretion on the part of the team member.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't even try to establish that. I only tried to get an explanation, a clarification, how many visual matches were made on the Srebrenica material. I have a letter in my expert report that I will try to retell. They say that in thousands of cases, of course, not only relating to Srebrenica, visual corrections were put in the basis of our report. So I can't say in Srebrenica we had 1, 2, 3, 5.000 visual corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to move on now, please, to the voters lists of 1997 and 1998, and as briefly as you can, can you tell us, if you know, how they were compiled.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Voters lists are lists of over-18 residents of Bosnia and Herzegovina who volunteered to be registered to vote in 1997 and 1998. They could register from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from various municipalities, or municipalities where they resided in 1991, and they could register also from abroad. So those are lists of people who voluntarily registered to participate in elections, and who were over 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Are the lists, as it were, area specific? Do they relate to a municipality, each list?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were area specific, because there is a certain procedure within the municipality. There is a certain place where you vote. It's not just one place in a municipality. Those lists are made not only for these elections. Though, there existed voters lists from 1991. They were obviously unusable. That's why the list of population, the census, was used. It's an aid. It helps to see where the voters come from, which area, et cetera. Of course, it's not centralised. Later on, when you collect all the lists, it's centralised, but initially they referred to a specific municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the use of voters lists by the Prosecution demographers was for a different reason than the use of the census of 1991. The use of the voters lists was to show that people on missing persons lists were not alive; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how Dr. Brunborg defines it. Why am I using voters lists? To show that no one is alive among those who are on the Prosecution's list of 7.661 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to be fair. Dr. Brunborg found 9 people alive in his first study and around 20 in the second study, and he excluded them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, there was quite a lot of population movement between 1991 and 1997 in Bosnia, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did Dr. Brunborg, in trying to ascertain whether those are on missing persons lists from Srebrenica, check all the voters lists of 1997 or just some of them?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday not all the voters. Dr. Brunborg did not release his list to be compared to the voters of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I said yesterday people from Srebrenica could be found in Tuzla, Jajce, or other places. Dr. Brunborg reduced the comparison between the lists to the boundaries, and I cannot tell you which boundaries exactly because it's not defined, to the boundaries of the municipality with which he compared Srebrenica as he defined -- or, rather, didn't define it, and he says -- he says there is a large degree of overlap. The key is bad. We have to bear in mind that voters lists do not include father's name, and if you release your own list without that piece of information, but not under 71 criteria, and I don't know how many criteria Dr. Brunborg used with voters lists because he doesn't say so, he just provides the list to be compared with the list of population. He evaluates, and he says due to a great amount of overlap, we had to reduce the comparison of voters lists to the territory of Srebrenica. Perhaps I didn't quote it very well, and it's not a proper quotation. I would have to find the passage to give you the exact words. And this automatically excluded from Dr. Brunborg's lists many people who were originally natives of Srebrenica, but at the moment when they registered to vote, lived either in other municipalities or they lived abroad. I said yesterday that only from Srebrenica municipality I found voters who had been in Srebrenica in 1991, and in 1997-1998, registered to vote in Sarajevo, Tuzla, Jajce, et cetera. Those voters were not taken into account by Dr. Brunborg when he compared with his own list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: To simplify this, I'm going to ask that 3D398 be put on the e-court, page 15 in the English and page 14 in the B/C/S, please. And so that you can remind yourself of the quote that you took from his report, it's at the very bottom of the page, Dr. Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. Should I read it so that we get the exact quote?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Read it to yourself or out loud. I don't really mind.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what Dr. Brunborg says, I quote: "A match of missing people and registered voters was not accepted if the locations were clearly inconsistent. For example, if a person was born, lived, and went missing in Eastern Bosnia, according to the missing lists, but registered to vote in and for a municipality in a completely different part of the country, according to the voters list." So a match was not accepted if that person was born and lived in Eastern Bosnia in 1991 and was found to have registered to vote in Sarajevo or some other place which was not in Eastern Bosnia, and of course abroad, and voters abroad could also register to vote. So these matches were not accepted. You could live in the municipalities considered by Dr. Brunborg to be Srebrenica, and you could only register to vote there, or, rather, these are the only data or the only voters that he took into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Dr. Radovanovic, is the effect of that that the list of dead and missing contains entries where other information from voters lists would tend to show that those people were alive and well but just living in another part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had Dr. Brunborg applied all the criteria that he applied in comparing the data with the census, he would have found quite a few of the people who were still alive. But Dr. Brunborg applied the strictest possible key. Not only that, he also restricts the area where he does the matching process. I can't really tell you what results would have been obtained had proper methodology been applied. The only thing I can tell you is that Dr. Brunborg committed two methodological errors, did things that were unacceptable in methodological terms, because he took the same statistical mass, the same statistical research, and in one part he applied a broad spectrum of keys, and in the other he did not. That's partiality, and it cannot be justified in methodological terms at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I object to this. Again, the same, it is that the answer went well beyond the question that was asked of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm nearly at the end of my examination of this witness. I'm still nonplussed by the objection, but I'll move on. I wonder if we could put P2413 into e-court, please. I'd like page 20 in the English and I think page 22 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In case you've still got a hard copy somewhere near you, Dr. Radovanovic, that would be easier to read, it's table 4 in Dr. Brunborg's 2005 report. It's at the bottom of the page in B/C/S and at the top in English.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
